figures.alt: Photo of a Michigan field in early morning with the Sun low behind a row of trees, and long tree shadows stretching across the grass toward the viewer.
figures.caption: When the Sun is low, shadows are long and point away from the Sun.

figures.alt: Photo of the Milky Way and many stars over a dark lakeshore with pine trees in silhouette.
figures.caption: The night sky changes by season because Earth orbits the Sun.

figures.alt: Photo of a pencil stuck in clay on a white paper in strong sunlight, with its long shadow falling across the paper.
figures.caption: The shadow-clock kit: mark the tip of the shadow at different times and see how its length and direction change.

figures.alt: Top view of a 10 centimeter stick with five shadow arrows to scale. 8:30 am: 34 cm pointing west. 10:00 am: 20 cm northwest. 12:00 pm: 9 cm north, the shortest. 2:00 pm: 18 cm northeast. 3:30 pm: 30 cm pointing east. The shadow points away from the Sun, which is in the south at noon, and is longest when the Sun is low.
figures.caption: The shadow table from this page drawn from above. Both the length and the direction change through the day.

figures.alt: Bar graph of shadow length of a 10 cm stick with direction. 8:30 am: 34 cm, west. 10:00 am: 20 cm, northwest. 12:00 pm: 9 cm, north. 2:00 pm: 18 cm, northeast. 3:30 pm: 30 cm, east. Shortest at noon.
figures.caption: Shadow of a 10 cm stick on a sunny day in about March or September. The shadow is shortest at noon (9 cm, pointing north) and long in the morning and afternoon. It points west in the morning and east in the afternoon, away from the Sun.
